item.title: I Automated My Communication, and Everything Worked. Then I Slowly Disappeared
item.content:encoded: AI can make communication faster, cleaner, and more reliable. But when too much of it is delegated, something harder to measure can disappear: the feeling that a real person is present. This piece explores the hidden cost of automating communication too far.

item.title: The Stablecoin Gold Rush Has a Plot Twist
item.content:encoded: Rather than competing to issue stablecoins, major asset managers are positioning themselves to manage the reserves backing them. The article argues that the GENIUS Act created an entirely new asset management category, prompting firms like BlackRock, Fidelity, State Street, Goldman Sachs, BNY, and Invesco to launch or file stablecoin reserve funds that could become foundational infrastructure for a multi-trillion-dollar digital dollar ecosystem

item.title: Developing Engineering Judgment in the Age of AI Code Generation
item.content:encoded: The article argues that AI is changing the role of software engineers rather than replacing them. As code generation becomes increasingly automated, developers who excel at system design, verification, architecture, communication, and mentorship will remain in demand, while companies must rethink how they train the next generation of engineers.

item.title: What Five Years in Banking Taught Me About Building Consumer Apps
item.content:encoded: Drawing on experience in both banking and children's mobile apps, the article explores which product management skills transfer across industries. It argues that fintech builds rigor around trust, metrics, and stakeholder management, while consumer products sharpen experimentation, emotional design, and observational research, making the combination particularly valuable for modern product leaders.

item.title: Crypto Portfolio Tracking Is Broken. It Needs to Become Action-Aware.
item.content:encoded: Otomato is a portfolio-aware DeFi assistant that helps crypto users monitor positions across DeFi, perps, prediction markets, tokens, and NFTs. Instead of forcing users to refresh dashboards manually, it sends low-noise alerts when something important changes.

item.title: Albert Dadon Is Building Financial Rails No Single Government Can Switch Off
item.content:encoded:
The thesis: AEREDIUM founder Albert Dadon argues the 2022 SWIFT disconnection was misread as a political story when it was an engineering one — credible neutrality can't be voted into existence, it has to be constructed.
The mechanism: AEREDIUM is a privacy-preserving Layer 1 ("the Trust Layer") that pushes rule-enforcement into attested hardware and threshold cryptography, so no single party — including the company — can override it unilaterally.
"A key nobody holds": its signing system (AERKey, formerly AEGISKey) uses threshold ECDSA (CGGMP24) where the key exists only as distributed shares that never assemble — making unilateral disclosure impossible while keeping legitimate legal process workable.
The seams thesis: Dadon points to the ~$290M KelpDAO exploit — where a single verifier, not the smart contract, was the weak link — as proof that the money is lost at the seams between systems.
The honest risk: the institutions that most need neutral rails (their procurement runs in years) are the slowest to adopt them — so AEREDIUM is pacing capital to be "ready when they arrive."

item.title: OLTP vs OLAP: Why Your App Database Isn't Built for Analytics
item.content:encoded: OLTP databases like PostgreSQL are optimized for fast reads and writes on specific records - orders, users, payments. OLAP databases like ClickHouse are built for a different job: aggregating and analyzing millions of rows at once. The same SQL query that takes minutes in PostgreSQL runs in seconds in ClickHouse, thanks to columnar storage. The two systems complement each other - PostgreSQL stores your application data, ClickHouse handles analytics on top of it.

item.title: I Built a PC Monitor That Learns Your Hardware
item.content:encoded:
Every traditional PC monitor — Afterburner, HWiNFO, CCleaner, GeForce Experience — runs on absolute thresholds and general profiles. "If temp over 80, alert." But your machine isn't in any table: silicon lottery, component aging, ambient temperature, and load composition mean a generic profile describes a computer you don't own. The fix is statistics on YOUR history, not the manufacturer's spec — median + MAD with Nelson Rules (the same Statistical Process Control factories use), workload-bucketed thermal baselines via Welford's algorithm, all running locally and offline with zero telemetry. A PSU rail sagging to 11.7V is "in spec" to a threshold but a 5-sigma anomaly against your own learned 11.95-12.05V norm — caught months before failure. Not a chatbot bolted on. Real statistics that don't hallucinate. It's working open-source code in PC Workman v1.7.9, built solo over 11 months between physical-labor shifts.
